The reproductive biology of Saurida undosquamis in the Parangipettai coastal waters has been studied extensively under the prevailing thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a temperature typical for coastal waters in this region of the family Synodontidae's distribution. At this temperature, gravid females at a body mass of 290 grams exhibit a total spawning output of approximately 217 eggs per day , calculated from annual production over 365 days at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. In contrast, smaller individuals weighing 97 grams produce roughly 54 eggs per day  under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. The species follows an iteroparous reproductive strategy, with females attaining puberty at a total length of 19.8 cm [Lp = 19.8 cm]. The corresponding wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is remarkably low at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a figure derived from the typical egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters, which reflects the small pelagic propagules characteristic of this synodontid fish. These larvae drift as ichthyoplankton before settling into a benthic existence.

Sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is pronounced in Brushtooth lizardfish, with females achieving a substantially larger maximum length than males. The maximum total length recorded for females reaches 48.9 cm [Li = 48.9 cm], while males stop growing at a considerably smaller 42.2 cm [Li = 42.2 cm]. This size disparity is mirrored in the corresponding maximum wet weights, which are derived from the length-weight relationship established for the species. The ultimate wet weight for females is 849 grams [Wwi = 849 grams], whereas males attain a peak body mass of only 532 grams [Wwi = 532 grams]. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is common among predatory teleosts and is often linked to the fecundity advantages conferred by larger body cavities, which allow for the accommodation of greater ovarian mass and thus higher egg production per spawning season.

Longevity estimates for Saurida undosquamis in the warm waters of the Parangipettai region indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately seven years. Under the ambient water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that characterizes this tropical habitat, the oldest documented individuals reach an age of 2555 days [am = 2555 days]. This lifespan is typical of medium-sized demersal fishes that do not exhibit extreme longevity, and it reflects a life-history strategy that balances relatively rapid growth with moderate reproductive investment over several years. The onset of reproductive maturity occurs well before this maximum age, allowing multiple spawning seasons across an individual's life. Mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age validation have confirmed this age structure in local populations, with very few individuals surviving past the seventh year due to natural mortality from predation and fishing pressure.

Comparative analysis of reproductive output relative to maternal body size reveals a clear positive relationship in this species. At the ambient temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that prevails in Parangipettai waters, a female at 290 grams produces roughly 217 eggs daily , which is approximately four times the daily production of a 97-gram female, which spawns about 54 eggs per day . This scaling of fecundity with maternal mass underscores the selective advantage of large body size in females, as larger individuals contribute disproportionately more offspring to the next generation. The relationship is not strictly isometric, however, suggesting that factors such as ovarian vascularization and metabolic constraints may moderate the increase in reproductive output with size. Such size-dependent fecundity has been documented across a range of marine fishes and is a key component in stock-recruitment models.

The hatchling mass of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] places Saurida undosquamis among the species producing the smallest pelagic larvae within the family Synodontidae. This exceptionally low wet weight at birth is a direct consequence of the small pelagic eggs, which measure about 0.9 millimeters in diameter, that the species produces. The tiny size of the propagules necessitates a brief lecithotrophic phase during which the yolk-sac larva relies on endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding on planktonic prey. The period of rapid larval growth that follows is critical for survival, as the small initial size makes the larvae vulnerable to a wide array of planktonic predators. Mortality during this stage is extremely high, a common pattern among marine fishes that produce numerous small pelagic eggs as part of a high-fecundity, low-survivorship life-history strategy.
